article.title: SpaceX's 13th Starship Test Flight Deploys First Working Starlink V3 Satellites, but Booster Suffers Hard Splashdown
article.summary: SpaceX's second Starship V3 test flight deployed the rocket's first functioning Starlink V3 satellites and returned Starship intact, though the booster suffered a hard splashdown.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

SpaceX flew the second test flight of its upgraded Starship V3 vehicle on July 24, lifting off from Starbase, Texas, at 6:51 p.m. Eastern and deploying the rocket's first batch of functioning third-generation Starlink satellites, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/). The Starship upper stage came down intact in the Indian Ocean, while the Super Heavy booster suffered a "hard" splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico after several of its engines failed to restart for landing, according to [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/25/super-heavy-starship-rocket-chalks-up-mostly-successful-test-flight/).

## What We Know

- Flight 13 was the second flight of Starship V3, the upgraded version of the vehicle SpaceX intends to use for future orbital missions, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/).
- As on Flight 12, SpaceX did not attempt to bring the Super Heavy booster back to the launch pad, instead targeting a "soft" splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico, [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/) reported. SpaceX acknowledged that not all of the Raptor engines needed for the landing burn started up, and [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/25/super-heavy-starship-rocket-chalks-up-mostly-successful-test-flight/) reported that only 10 of 13 engines restarted, with just five still running at the moment of splashdown — sending the booster into the water at a higher speed than planned and producing what Spaceflight Now called a "hard" splashdown.
- The Starship upper stage fared better. It reentered belly-first before flipping upright for a rocket-powered splashdown northwest of Australia, remaining intact with several of its onboard cameras still working, according to [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/25/super-heavy-starship-rocket-chalks-up-mostly-successful-test-flight/). [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/) separately put the splashdown at approximately 65.5 minutes after liftoff and likewise reported the vehicle came down intact rather than exploding.
- The mission deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites — the first time a Starship flight carried functioning satellites rather than mass simulators — using a "Pez-like payload dispenser" that released them one at a time from a slot near the nose, according to [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/25/super-heavy-starship-rocket-chalks-up-mostly-successful-test-flight/). Six of the satellites were fitted with cameras to inspect the Starship's heat shield tiles and general condition after separation, Spaceflight Now reported.
- The satellites underwent about 20 minutes of testing after deployment, including solar array and antenna deployment and communications checks with ground stations and other Starlink satellites, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/). SpaceX said: "We've successfully communicated with all sats using RF [radio-frequency] and laser links and been able to download key telemetry."
- Starship also briefly relit one of its Raptor engines in space for about 14 seconds, longer than on previous tests, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/); [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/25/super-heavy-starship-rocket-chalks-up-mostly-successful-test-flight/) reported the maneuver demonstrates a restart capability required for future lunar missions.
- The flight followed a scrapped July 16 attempt, when four of the booster's 33 Raptor engines failed to ignite properly, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/) and [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/25/super-heavy-starship-rocket-chalks-up-mostly-successful-test-flight/). SpaceX later said the failure was caused by liquid-oxygen turbopump problems: moisture had accumulated in the pumps and frozen on contact with the cryogenic propellant, slowing or stopping them, [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/) reported.
- After the abort, SpaceX pulled both the Starship upper stage, Ship 40, and the Super Heavy booster, Booster 20, for repairs, replacing multiple Raptor engines before restacking the vehicle by July 22, according to [Spaceflight Now](https://spaceflightnow.com/2026/07/23/live-coverage-spacex-ready-for-2nd-attempt-to-launch-starship-flight-13-following-post-abort-engine-work/). A second launch attempt was then waved off for weather as Tropical Storm Bertha moved through Texas, before SpaceX retargeted Friday, July 24, Spaceflight Now reported. The eventual launch slipped roughly a day further because of cloudy conditions that would have prevented imaging of the vehicle during ascent, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/).
- SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said that if Flight 13 went well, the company might attempt the first orbital Starship mission on Flight 14, followed by the first launch of the vehicle from Florida on Flight 15, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/spacex-conducts-13th-starship-test-flight/).

## What We Don't Know

- Neither SpaceNews nor Spaceflight Now detailed why the booster's landing engines failed to fully restart, beyond confirming that not all of the needed Raptors started up — a separate issue from the July 16 turbopump icing problem.
- Shotwell's comments on Flight 14 attempting an orbital mission were conditional on Flight 13 going well; no date has been set for either Flight 14 or Flight 15.
- No findings from the six heat-shield-inspection satellites' camera data have been reported yet.

The mission follows Starship's grounding after Flight 12, when the FAA declared a mishap after the Super Heavy booster failed its boostback burn and hard-splashed, halting flights pending a Raptor 3 investigation, as [previously reported](/article/2026-05/29-faa-declares-starship-flight-12-a-mishap-and-grounds-the-rocket-pending-raptor-3-engine-investigation).
